Thanks — I checked these before responding.

- #36640 covers the **always keep one model** behavior through the old `OPENCODE_AGENTS_SWITCH_SINGLE_MODEL` flag. That addresses the pinned-model side, but not the case where untouched agents should use their own configured model and variant.
- #41221, #39319, and #35899 cover the inverse failure: an explicit manual choice is discarded by agent/session state changes.
- #41387 is adjacent but concerns delivery of the previous agent's system prompt, not model-selection precedence.

The closest implementation work is #40604. It tags a manual model selection with the agent under which it was made, so an untouched agent can use its configured default without destroying a deliberate override. That is the same ambiguity this issue is trying to resolve rather than choosing “always switch” or “always preserve.”

The remaining distinction is client/runtime scope: #40604 currently changes the app composer (`packages/app/...`), while this report reproduces in the OpenCode 2 beta TUI. The useful V2 behavior would be:

1. An agent with no explicit session override uses its configured model and variant when selected.
2. A deliberate model/variant selection remains an explicit override instead of being silently discarded.
3. The UI indicates the override and offers a direct way to clear it and return to the agent default.

I'm happy for maintainers to consolidate this under an existing issue if the equivalent V2 TUI path is tracked there. The main point is that the state needs to distinguish an inherited agent default from an explicit user selection; a single unlabelled session model cannot satisfy both sets of reports.

I'd like to work on this one.

On `origin/v2` the tool lives at `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/subagent.ts`: the `agent` input is a free-form string with no catalog of valid IDs, so models guess (e.g. `explorer` vs the actual `explore`).

Plan: at plugin registration (where `Agent.Service` is already available), list the Location's agents, filter to subagent-capable ones (`mode !== "primary"`, not `hidden`), and append a compact `id: description` catalog to the `agent` input field description (and/or the tool description). The catalog is therefore Location-specific and mode-aware; per-caller permission filtering stays at execution time via the existing `permission.assert` in `execute`.

Targeting `v2` (the issue reproduces on `opencode2`), with a regression test asserting the surfaced catalog.

Worth noting there's a complementary approach if you want *conversation* rather than dictation: [qwen-audio-agent](https://github.com/QwenAudio/qwen-audio-agent) (disclosure: I maintain it) runs a full-duplex voice frontend in front of CLI agents including OpenCode:

Issue Description
When using OpenCode to call GPT-5.6-luna, intermittent failures occur:

Sometimes it responds normally;
Other times it returns the error: Upstream request failed: [403] This model is not available in your region.
Troubleshooting Process
Checked router rule matching: Found that OpenCode requests sometimes fail to match any proxy/routing rules, making it impossible to determine whether the traffic actually went through the proxy.
Checked network connection method: Discovered that OpenCode establishes connections using IPv4 + IPv6 dual-stack.
Identified the cause of rule failure: The proxy/routing rules on the router cannot match or hijack IPv6 traffic. This portion of traffic exits directly using the real IP (direct connection).
Root Cause Analysis
When OpenCode connects via IPv4, traffic is captured by router rules and forced through the proxy, so it can be accessed normally.

When OpenCode connects via IPv6, traffic bypasses proxy rules and exits via direct connection. The server detects that the real IP's region is restricted and returns a 403 region restriction error.

Solution
Disable IPv6 on the computer to force OpenCode to establish connections only via IPv4.

This ensures all traffic is handled by the router's proxy rules, and the 403 region-unavailable issue caused by IPv6 direct connection no longer occurs.

Summary
IPv6 traffic bypasses router proxy rules → Real IP is exposed → Triggers region restriction 403.

Disabling client IPv6 and forcing pure IPv4 connections unifies all traffic through the proxy, which completely resolves this issue.

Thanks for the thorough fix — tracking bytes/chunks at the executor seam is exactly the right layer, and `withStreamDiagnostics` wrapping the response is cleaner than handling it ad hoc at each call site.

One thing worth double-checking before merge: the error-kind change may alter retry/continuation semantics for mid-stream failures.

**Before this PR**, a body read failure surfaced as `InvalidProviderOutput` with `classification: "incomplete-stream"`. In `packages/core/src/session/runner/llm.ts:472-481`, that classification is specifically checked:

```ts
const incompleteStream =
  llmFailure?.reason._tag === "InvalidProviderOutput" &&
  llmFailure.reason.classification === "incomplete-stream"
if (llmError && incompleteStream && record.outputStarted && toolsAllowContinuation)
  return CallOutcome.Continue({...})
```

So a mid-stream failure after output had started was treated as a partial success and **continued**, not re-run.

**After this PR**, the same failure becomes `Transport` (the `openai-chat.test.ts` assertion change confirms it). In `packages/core/src/session/runner/retry.ts:17-37`, `Transport` is unconditionally retryable:

```ts
case "Transport":
  return true
```

while `InvalidProviderOutput` only retries for `incomplete-stream`. So a stream that failed after emitting output will now be **discarded and retried from scratch** (up to 4 exponential attempts) instead of continued — losing the partial output and potentially re-invoking tools.

Two options to consider:

1. Keep the read failure as `InvalidProviderOutput:incomplete-stream` but enrich its `http` context with the new diagnostics (bytes/chunks/requestId/status). The issue asks for structured diagnostics, not necessarily a tag change.
2. Or, if `Transport` is intentional, gate the continuation logic on `record.outputStarted` + a `Transport` read failure so partial output is still continued rather than retried.

Also minor: `kind: "DecodeError:Error:ECONNRESET"` concatenates the error class name — for non-Error causes the middle segment is `Error`, which reads a bit ambiguously in logs. A bounded cause-chain array might be clearer, but that's cosmetic.

This is a behavior regression for users who intentionally wait through provider capacity/rate-limit shortages. Before this PR, retryable provider failures with explicit Retry-After / retry-after-ms could keep retrying until the provider recovered. After this PR, all high-level session retries are forced to stop after 5 attempts, even when the provider is explicitly telling the client to wait and retry.

The hard cap is too blunt, and there is no config/opt-out in opencode.json to restore the previous behavior. That makes this a user-visible breaking change for long-running sessions and enterprise/custom providers where transient capacity shortages can last longer than five seconds or five retry windows.

Please either make the retry limit configurable, including an unlimited option, or scope the cap only to locally computed exponential retries without provider retry headers. Explicit provider retry headers should not be treated the same as blind infinite retry loops.

Additional Windows/Desktop evidence from OpenCode 1.18.18:

- The freeze consistently followed deleting a session. In one incident, `main.log` stopped at 08:40:57.533 and `renderer.log` stopped at 08:41:01.113. No Electron unresponsive event/recovery dialog, Crashpad dump, or Windows AppHang/AppCrash event appeared; the sidecar continued independently.
- A no-deletion control session survived 34+ minutes and saw ResizeObserver bursts up to 326/min, while the frozen session peaked around 147/min. ResizeObserver volume alone is therefore not sufficient.
- The delete path is: `packages/app/src/pages/session/timeline/message-timeline.tsx:865-925` calls the session DELETE endpoint, updates the client session list, evicts cached data, and dispatches tab removal. The server path reaches `packages/opencode/src/session/session.ts:608-625`, which cancels matching background jobs, publishes `session.deleted`, and removes the event aggregate. `packages/core/src/event.ts:514-523` deletes the event sequence and event rows in a transaction.
- The post-delete renderer cleanup reaches `packages/app/src/context/tabs.tsx:298-349`, which updates persisted tab/closed/info state. Desktop persistence ultimately reaches `packages/desktop/src/main/ipc.ts:124-126`, where `electron-store.set()` is called synchronously on the Electron main process.

This makes a main-process persistence stall a plausible explanation for the simultaneous Desktop freeze, but I cannot yet prove which individual write blocks or how long it takes. One correction to earlier speculation: `packages/app/src/context/notification.tsx` handles `session.idle`/`session.error` and prunes to 500 entries/30 days; it does not directly handle `session.deleted`, so the notification list should not be treated as the confirmed delete trigger.

The SQLite cleanup I performed locally preserved all 121 sessions and removed only 26 orphan events, 2 orphan event sequences, and 2 stale runtime directories; post-clean integrity checks passed. It did not delete sessions or establish the Desktop freeze root cause.

Could this be triaged as a Windows Desktop session-delete/persistence hang, with instrumentation or a regression test around the delete-to-tab-persistence path?

Concrete fix proposal:

1. Do not apply the hard 5-attempt cap to provider-directed retries. If the API error has `retry-after` or `retry-after-ms`, the provider is explicitly telling the client to wait and retry. That should not be treated the same as a blind infinite exponential loop.

2. Add a user-visible config knob instead of hard-coding this behavior. For example:

```jsonc
{
  "retry": {
    "max_retries": 5,
    "provider_retry_after_max_retries": false
  }
}
```

or a simpler first pass:

```jsonc
{
  "retry": { "max_retries": 5 } // number | false, where false means unlimited
}
```

3. Thread that config into `SessionRetry.policy(...)` from `packages/opencode/src/session/processor.ts` instead of relying on `RETRY_MAX_RETRIES` as an unconfigurable constant.

4. Minimal behavior change if you want to keep the current default:

```ts
const headers = SessionV1.APIError.isInstance(error) ? error.data.responseHeaders : undefined
const hasProviderRetryAfter = !!headers?.["retry-after"] || !!headers?.["retry-after-ms"]
if (!hasProviderRetryAfter && meta.attempt > maxRetries) return Cause.done(meta.attempt)
```

5. Tests that should be added:

- retryable 503/429 without retry headers stops at the configured default
- APIError with `retry-after-ms` continues past the default cap
- APIError with `retry-after` continues past the default cap
- `retry.max_retries = false` preserves the previous unlimited behavior
- `retry.max_retries = N` caps at N for non-provider-directed retries

The important distinction is: local exponential retries need a safety cap; provider-directed retry headers need either unlimited behavior or a separate user-configurable cap. Right now this PR collapses both cases into one hard-coded limit, which is the regression.

Since they have introduced models with 15/30 $ limits, the 60 $ monthly budget claim is completely misleading. If you max out a 15 $ model, your monthly usage is 100%. 

Basically you have to multiply the costs of a model by the factor 60/Limit and sum it up. Then you get the real costs, that are charged on the 60$ budget.

Example:
Deepseek V4 Flash 15 $ Limit -> Factor 4
Mimo 2.5 60$ Limit -> Factor 1

Costs shown on usage dasboard:
Deepseek 10 $
Mimo 5 $

10 x 4 + 5 x 1 = 45 $

45/60 = **75%**

Same problem here.

Adding the numbers from my account, since the console only shows percentages and they have to be converted against the documented limits before the inconsistency is visible.

**Console** (<https://opencode.ai/auth>), read at **2026-08-18 10:36 UTC**:

| card | shown | resets in | implied window start | dollars, at the documented limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Continuous (5 h) | 0% | 5 h 0 m | 2026-08-18 08:36 UTC | $0.00 – $0.12 (of $12) |
| Weekly | 7% | 5 d 13 h | 2026-08-16 23:36 UTC | $2.10 – $2.40 (of $30) |
| Monthly | **17%** | 29 d 8 h | 2026-08-16 18:36 UTC | **$10.20 – $10.80** (of $60) |

Window starts are derived from the reset counters; limits from <https://opencode.ai/docs/go/>. Ranges assume the percentage is truncated to an integer. One corroboration that the derived anchors are real: the monthly window starts 2026-08-16 18:36 UTC, and my `auth.json` — the moment I subscribed and saved the API key — was written at 18:55 UTC the same day. The month is counted from the subscription.

**CLI**, same account, all time (`opencode stats`): **$2.96**, 88 sessions, 402 messages, 1.5M input / 85.5K output / 5.8M cache read.

Every costed message, by hour — the entire history of the account fits in this table:

| hour (UTC+2) | cost | running total from here to now |
|---|---|---|
| 08-15 17:00 → 08-16 19:00 | $0.0000 | $2.9606 |
| 08-16 20:00 | $0.0196 | $2.9606 |
| 08-16 21:00 | $2.1072 | $2.9410 |
| 08-16 22:00 | $0.0813 | $0.8337 |
| 08-17 10:00 | $0.1710 | $0.7525 |
| 08-17 12:00 | $0.0986 | $0.5815 |
| 08-17 13:00 | $0.4829 | $0.4829 |

Last request 2026-08-17 11:52 UTC; nothing since, which the 0% on the 5-hour card confirms. This is the only machine I have ever run OpenCode on, and there is no activity of any kind before 2026-08-15 15:08 UTC.

**Why the monthly figure can't be right.** This needs no assumption about server-side pricing, and no trust in the CLI's estimates beyond their order of magnitude:

- The monthly window *contains* the weekly one — both end now, the monthly starts earlier — so `monthly − weekly` is exactly the usage between the two window starts.
- The console puts that difference at **≥ $7.80** ($10.20 − $2.40, taking the most favourable rounding in both directions).
- Everything this account has ever spent is **$2.96**, and $2.94 of it landed in one evening that sits inside *both* windows.

So the monthly card reports, as a difference between two nested windows, roughly **2.6× more than the account has spent in total**. No interval of time on this account can hold it. The weekly and 5-hour cards are in the right range.

**Possible cause.** The two cards become consistent if the monthly one divides by the wrong limit. For a single underlying figure `X`:

- `X / $30` displaying as 7% → `X ∈ [$2.10, $2.40)`
- `X / $12` displaying as 17% → `X ∈ [$2.04, $2.16)`

Both hold at once for `X ∈ [$2.10, $2.16)`, and the CLI's figure for that period sits right inside it: **$2.1072** for the single hour that is 71% of my lifetime spend. So if the Monthly card computed its percentage against the **5-hour limit ($12)** instead of the monthly limit ($60), it would print exactly the 17% I see, from the same dollars that make the weekly card print 7%. That would make it a display bug rather than over-counted usage — but from outside, with only percentages exposed, I can't tell which.

**#35306** — That issue is about the description text of the existing "Move session" dialog being unclear. Our `/cd` is a different UX: a lightweight slash command with inline path input, not the full directory-picker dialog. Both use the same `moveSession` API, but `/cd` is for quick switching (e.g. between worktrees) without navigating a list. The `change_directory` agent tool is a separate addition that doesn't exist today — agents currently have no way to switch directories at all.

**#38456** — That issue is about `!cd` (shell command) not updating the statusline. Our feature calls `moveSession` directly (which updates session state server-side) and refreshes VCS state, so the statusline reflects the new directory. Different problem, different mechanism.

Reproduced on `0.0.0-beta-17498` on macOS arm64. This also affects `service stop`, not only `service restart`.

The setup uses separate XDG homes and fixed ports for isolated services, then `exec`s the underlying `opencode2` command.

Observed sequence:

1. Service PID `29234` owned its configured listener.
2. Ran `opencode service stop`.
3. The listener closed, but PID `29234` remained alive in `Ss` state and was reparented to PID 1.
4. The process still held `opencode-next.db`, `opencode-next.db-wal`, and `opencode-next.db-shm` open.
5. Starting the service created PID `93758`, which opened the same database and assumed the configured listener.

At that point the machine had 18 `serve --service` processes but only three listeners. The stale processes covered multiple isolated XDG homes and included both `0.0.0-next-17444` and `0.0.0-beta-17498`.

Sending `SIGTERM` to the 15 confirmed non-listening processes did not terminate any of them. Some changed from `Ss` to `Rs`, but all remained alive. `SIGKILL` was required.

After removing the stale processes:

- Exactly three expected service processes remained.
- Each owned one expected listener.
- All active MCP connections were healthy.
- Active local MCP process trees remained attached to the current service.

There was also a correctness impact beyond memory usage. Two remote MCP servers began failing OAuth refresh with:

> Refresh token is invalid or has already been claimed by another client.

Removing the stale credentials, authenticating sequentially, and killing the non-listening daemons restored both MCPs. I cannot prove the stale daemons caused the token claim race, but they were concurrently holding the same database and MCP state when it occurred.

This appears to be the same lifecycle bug reported here, still present in `beta-17498`. The stop path should verify that the old daemon and its process tree have exited before returning success.
